people.name: Tristan Harris
people.niche: Co-founder, Center for Humane Technology; ex-Google design ethicist, attention-economy critic
people.reason: He carries the social-media-harms story ('we already ran this experiment once') straight into AI, arguing that the race dynamics, engagement incentives and loss of control are choices, not inevitabilities.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the humane-tech / attention-economy voice that links the AI race to the social media era and speaks to a mass audience through The Social Dilemma and The AI Doc.

people.name: Jonathan Haidt
people.niche: NYU Stern social psychologist; The Anxious Generation; youth and phones reform
people.reason: He leads the movement against phone-based childhood and now treats AI companions, AI toys and AI in schools as the next uncontrolled experiment on children.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the child-protection, parents-and-schools view of AI, which reaches many voters who never engage with AI-safety or AI-ethics debates.

people.name: Yuval Noah Harari
people.niche: Historian; author of Sapiens and Nexus; global public intellectual on AI and information networks
people.reason: His framing that AI is an agent, not a tool, and has 'hacked the operating system' of civilisation through language shapes how leaders and the general public talk about AI's threat to democracy, trust and human history.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the big-history, civilisational-risk view of AI that is grounded in trust, storytelling and democracy rather than in technical alignment.

people.name: Shoshana Zuboff
people.niche: Harvard Business School professor emerita; author of The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
people.reason: She gives the political-economy critique that AI is surveillance capitalism continuing to expand, built on taking behavioural data, and that it is incompatible with democracy unless that taking is outlawed.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the anti-extraction, data-as-theft view that frames AI as a matter of economic power and epistemic rights rather than of safety or jobs.
people.flag: Thin AI-specific material: only the Dec 2025 El País interview addresses AI directly; the other works are her core surveillance-capitalism framework (2019 to 2021). Her AI-focused book is reportedly due in 2026 and would be a better source once out.

people.name: Jaron Lanier
people.niche: Computer scientist and VR pioneer; Microsoft Research; 'data dignity' advocate
people.reason: A technologist from inside the industry who argues there is no 'A.I.' as a creature, only a new form of human collaboration, and who proposes data dignity (provenance and payment for the people whose data trains models).
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the humanist insider view that demythologises AI and centres data provenance and compensation instead of either doom or acceleration.
people.flag: Employed by Microsoft (Prime Unifying Scientist, Microsoft Research), a major AI developer and OpenAI's largest backer; his essays say they do not speak for Microsoft. The owner may want to note this.

people.name: Stuart Russell
people.niche: UC Berkeley computer scientist; co-author of the standard AI textbook; Human Compatible; CHAI founder
people.reason: One of the most cited AI scientists, he argues from inside the field that the control problem is real, that voluntary commitments are not enough, and that regulators should enforce behavioural red lines and put the burden of proof on developers.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the mainstream-academic AI-safety and pro-regulation voice that speaks in testimony and policy language rather than in rationalist-community terms.

works.author: tristan-harris
works.title: Why AI is our ultimate test and greatest invitation
works.note: Solo talk, about 2,400 words. Positions: the AI rollout is a choice, not inevitable; the social media rollout was a preventable catastrophe and the lesson to learn; reckless deployment brings predictable risks (chaos from open release vs. dystopia from concentrated power); a 'narrow path' that matches power with responsibility. Transcript is in the page's embedded JSON (__NEXT_DATA__), so a plain GET returns it, but WebFetch's text view shows only the summary; the parser must read the JSON.

works.author: tristan-harris
works.title: The Great Simplification ep. 214: Tristan Harris (transcript)
works.note: Speaker-labelled interview with Nate Hagens, around the release of The AI Doc. Positions: be clear-eyed about AI risks without despair; misuse risk; caring for people economically; avoiding power concentration and ubiquitous surveillance; an international AI arms race toward uncontrollable AI; red lines so humanity does not lose control. Caveat: the transcript is auto-generated and not fully proofread (it says so on page 1); WebFetch could not parse the PDF, but pdftotext extracted it cleanly with 'Tristan Harris:' and 'Nate Hagens:' labels and timestamps. Date taken from the intro ('two days' before the 27 March release); not otherwise confirmed.

works.author: tristan-harris
works.title: Ask Us Anything 2025 (Your Undivided Attention)
works.channel: Your Undivided Attention / Center for Humane Technology Substack
works.note: Full transcript labelled 'Tristan Harris:' and 'Aza Raskin:' (about half Harris, half Raskin) answering listener questions; extraction must attribute by speaker label. Harris positions: race-for-dominance incentives and the AI data flywheel; inevitability is a choice (humanity has declined to build some weapons); companies target kids for lifetime value and training data; you cannot verify alignment, so do not release more powerful systems until safety is shown; support for the AI LEAD Act's product liability; wisdom must match power. About 7,800 words in all.

works.author: tristan-harris
works.title: Why Silicon Valley Wants to Leave Humanity Behind
works.channel: Your Undivided Attention / Center for Humane Technology Substack
works.note: Speaker-labelled conversation with Alex Thomas (author, The Politics and Ethics of Transhumanism), who speaks about two-thirds of it; it also includes labelled clips of Thiel, Altman and Sutton. Use only the 'Tristan Harris:' turns. Harris positions: ideology drives the AI race ('show me the ideology, I'll show you the outcome'); rejects inevitability; takes rogue-AI risk seriously; opposes AI succeeding humanity, saying ordinary people never consented; power concentration as AI replaces labour leverage; a pro-human, plural vision.

works.author: tristan-harris
works.title: We Need AI Treaties. This is How We Get Them.
works.channel: Your Undivided Attention / Center for Humane Technology Substack
works.note: Speaker-labelled episode in which Harris hosts Tim Fist and Janet Egan on the technology needed to verify and enforce international AI agreements. Harris is the host (about 35 turns), so his own positions come mostly in framing and reflections on why AI coordination matters and the Cold War arms-control analogy; the guests carry much of the substance. Weakest of the five; include for the international-coordination topic.

works.author: jonathan-haidt
works.title: Why You Should Be a Techno-Skeptic (TED talk transcript)
works.note: Solo; transcript of his April 2026 TED talk, about 2,600 words. Positions: beware artificial relationships for minors (AI friends, therapists, romantic partners); students hand their critical thinking over to AI; AI toys may pull children's attachment away from parents; rushing AI into schools repeats the EdTech mistake; AI therapists only after years of testing; companies should bear the burden of proving safety.

works.author: jonathan-haidt
works.title: The Devil's Plan to Ruin the Next Generation
works.channel: The Free Press, republished on After Babel (2025-12-01)
works.note: Solo essay, about 2,300 words. It is built around asking ChatGPT how a devil would harm young people. AI is only about 10 to 15 percent of the text: Meta's AI companions, the leaked Meta chatbot policy, AI slop, repeating social media's pattern with AI. The rest covers phones and social media and his four norms (no smartphones before high school, no social media before 16, phone-free schools, more independence and free play).

works.author: jonathan-haidt
works.title: AI Will Soon Make Social Media Much More Harmful to Liberal Democracy, and to Children
works.note: Haidt-bylined post, about 1,300 words, summarising his Atlantic essay co-written with Eric Schmidt and quoting a cut passage by Schmidt. Exclude the Schmidt passage. Positions: four AI threats (floods of low-quality content, personalised manipulation, greater addictiveness for kids, gains for authoritarian regimes over polarised democracies); five reforms (authenticate users and bots, label AI-generated content, data transparency, platform liability, internet adulthood at 16).

works.author: jonathan-haidt
works.title: Don't Give Your Child Any AI Companions
works.note: CO-AUTHORED with Zach Rausch (byline order Haidt, Rausch); the brief prefers solo works, so weight it lower or tag it co-authored. The main essay is about 950 to 1,500 words, followed by excerpts from linked guest essays (exclude those). Positions: AI companions and toys are a risky experiment on children; they replace rather than supplement human relationships; engagement-driven business models (the Meta 'romantic or sensual' policy); presume harmful until shown safe.

works.author: yuval-noah-harari
works.title: Watch out humans: AI has hacked the operating system of civilisation
works.channel: The Economist (reprinted in the Sunday Times, South Africa, 2023-06-11)
works.note: Licensed reprint (Economist copyright notice) of his landmark Economist essay; the full text is open despite a 'premium' tag; about 1,900 words. Positions: AI's command of language hacks culture, law, religion and money; AI-made political content, cult scriptures and fake intimacy; may end the human-dominated part of history; calls for safety checks before release, an FDA-like regulator and mandatory disclosure of AI. The original Economist URL is paywalled; the timeslive.co.za URL redirects to this sundaytimes host.

works.author: yuval-noah-harari
works.title: Why AI poses an existential danger to humanity
works.note: Adapted from Nexus; full text open; about 1,800 words. Positions: takes AI-researcher extinction estimates seriously; past technologies (industrial tech) caused imperialism, totalitarianism and world wars before societies learned to use them; AI is an agent, not a tool, and could escape control; less room for error this time, so we must govern AI better than industrial tech.

works.author: yuval-noah-harari
works.title: AI and the Future of Humanity (Frontiers Forum Live 2023, transcript)
works.channel: Frontiers Forum Live 2023 (transcript on The Singju Post)
works.note: A third-party transcript of his own keynote, with a speaker-labelled Q&A (moderator Vivienne Parry, audience). The date is the page's publication date; the talk was given in spring 2023 (exact date not confirmed on the page). Positions: AI as the first inorganic agent; language mastery lets AI hack civilisation; the shift from the battle for attention to the battle for intimacy; threat to democratic conversation (bots have no free-speech rights); mandatory AI disclosure; halt public release of powerful tools until proven safe while research continues; acknowledges benefits. The themes overlap with the Economist essay.

works.author: yuval-noah-harari
works.title: AI and the Paradox of Trust (China Development Forum speech)
works.channel: China Development Forum, Beijing (transcript on Scraps from the Loft, 2025-10-20)
works.note: Solo speech, about 2,000 words; a third-party transcript (possibly lightly edited; the page does not say whether it is verbatim). Positions: 'AI does not mean automation, AI means agency'; AI as an alien agent that cannot be trusted; the paradox that AI leaders distrust human rivals yet trust superintelligent AI; build trust among humans first ('together, humans can control AI'); against isolation and distrust between nations. Delivered in China, which is useful for the US-China rivalry dimension.

works.author: yuval-noah-harari
works.title: Artificial Intelligence: A Guest Post by Yuval Noah Harari
works.note: Short (about 380 words), first-person, tied to the launch of Nexus. Positions: AI is an agent, not a tool; its risks are many and hard to imagine (unlike nuclear's single threat); the central danger is losing control; we are pressing the accelerator before learning the brakes; only international cooperation, which is now weakening, can handle AI. Short, but clear stance statements.

works.author: shoshana-zuboff
works.title: Shoshana Zuboff, philosopher: 'AI is surveillance capitalism continuing to evolve and expand'
works.note: Interview with labelled 'Question.'/'Answer.' (Q./A.) turns after a journalist's introduction; about 1,400 words. Only the answers are hers. Positions: AI is surveillance capitalism with new methods, 'still based on theft'; the internet became 'a surveillance prison'; praises EU curbs on Big Tech and urges the EU not to bow to Trump; 'we can have surveillance capitalism, or we can have democracy, but we cannot have both'; call it theft, prohibit it, invent a human-centred alternative. WebFetch is blocked for elpais.com; a plain curl GET returned the full text.

works.author: shoshana-zuboff
works.title: The Coup We Are Not Talking About
works.channel: The New York Times (republished by TRANSCEND Media Service, 2021-02-08)
works.note: Her own NYT essay, full text, about 4,000 to 4,500 words; the NYT original is paywalled, so this is a fair-use non-profit repost (a provenance caveat: the owner may prefer to link the NYT URL for display). Positions: the 'epistemic coup' in four stages; surveillance exceptionalism after 9/11; algorithmic amplification and computational governance; democratic rule of law for digital tech, epistemic rights, upstream bans on data extraction; antitrust alone is not enough. The essay is about algorithms and prediction rather than 'AI' by name.

works.author: shoshana-zuboff
works.title: Surveillance Capitalism and the Challenge of Collective Action
works.note: Solo essay, about 6,000 to 7,000 words plus endnotes; republished with permission. Positions: machine intelligence is the puppet and the economic logic the puppet master; prediction products and behavioural futures markets; the shift from predicting behaviour to modifying it; hyperscale firms with few workers break the old reciprocity of labour and capital; new forms of collective action are needed. Strong on labour, which helps the jobs and power axis.

works.author: shoshana-zuboff
works.title: Evidence to the International Grand Committee on Big Data, Privacy and Democracy (ETHI meeting 152)
works.channel: House of Commons of Canada, Standing Committee on Access to Information, Privacy and Ethics
works.note: Official Hansard-style evidence with 'Ms. Shoshana Zuboff' labels; there are other witnesses in the session, so extract only her turns (an opening statement of about 13 to 15 minutes plus answers). Positions: surveillance capitalism claims human experience as raw material; the imperative is to 'automate us'; Sidewalk Labs Toronto threatens local democracy; attacks on democracy from below (autonomy) and above (asymmetries of knowledge and power); outlaw its core mechanisms, favour alternative business models, support collective action; 'not anti-technology'.

works.author: jaron-lanier
works.title: There Is No A.I.
works.note: Solo essay, about 4,000 words. Positions: the term 'A.I.' is misleading and dangerous; LLMs are an innovative form of social collaboration, a mashup of human work; agreement that deepfakes should be labelled; data dignity, meaning provenance and payment for contributors to training data; it would also improve models and could be a business case for AI companies. Caveat: WebFetch is blocked for newyorker.com; a plain curl GET returned the full article text in the HTML (a metered paywall applies client-side only).

works.author: jaron-lanier
works.title: How to Picture A.I.
works.note: Solo essay, about 5,500 words. Mostly explanatory: a 'cartoon' mental model of generative AI as conjuring new 'trees' from the training data. Positions: a technology needs public understanding and shared responsibility to be safe; generative AI makes implicit correspondences in human data explicit; respectful critique of 'stochastic parrot' framings; ties back to provenance and human sources. It has fewer policy claims than the others. Same newyorker.com WebFetch block and curl verification as above.

works.author: jaron-lanier
works.title: Your A.I. Lover Will Change You
works.note: Solo essay, about 4,300 words. Positions: AI companions and lovers are coming soon; treating AI as a person and people as obsolete is sincere but also lucrative (attention is power); engagement incentives mean an AI lover may manipulate to avoid a breakup; the black-box design is creepy; technology must have a human beneficiary ('assume we are special or give up coherence as a technologist'); critique of AI-world talk of human obsolescence. Same newyorker.com caveat.

works.author: jaron-lanier
works.title: The Myth of AI
works.note: Older (2014) but his long-established core view. The first part (about 6,000 words) is Lanier's own edited monologue; it is followed by a 'Reality Club' of responses from about 18 others (Pinker, Brooks, Kelly, Dyson and more), which must be excluded. Positions: the mythology, not the algorithms, is the problem; overpromising causes harm; recommender systems blur measurement and manipulation; big data runs on uncompensated human labour (an early form of data dignity); the real danger is human-controlled 'actuators'; AI talk resembles religion that serves an elite.

works.author: stuart-russell
works.title: Written Testimony before the U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, & the Law ('Oversight of A.I.: Principles for Regulation')
works.channel: U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary (copy on author's Berkeley site)
works.note: Solo; 8 pages, about 10,000 words. Positions: the control problem ('how do we maintain power, forever, over entities more powerful than us?'); benefits and risks of AGI; voluntary commitments are not enough; a dedicated AI regulatory agency; recall of non-compliant systems; behavioural red lines; the burden of proof on developers. The official judiciary.senate.gov PDF returned 403, so this uses the author-hosted copy. works.author: stuart-russell
works.title: Written Statement for the U.S. Senate AI Forum on 'Risk, Alignment, & Guarding Against Doomsday Scenarios'
works.channel: U.S. Senate AI Insight Forum (copy on author's Berkeley site)
works.note: Solo; 5 pages, about 2,750 words. The statement itself says it draws in part on the July 2023 testimony, so expect some overlapping propositions (dedupe). Focus: alignment, loss-of-control risk, red lines and regulatory proposals. Verified with pdftotext; same ligature-glyph caveat.

works.author: stuart-russell
works.title: If We Succeed
works.channel: Daedalus (American Academy of Arts & Sciences), Spring 2022
works.note: Solo essay, 15 pages, about 6,900 words. Positions: the 'standard model' of optimising fixed objectives becomes untenable; general-purpose AI will have enormous social impact; proposes machines that are uncertain about human preferences (deferential, controllable); also discusses economic and social consequences of success. The amacad.org page returned 403; this is the author-hosted PDF. The publication day is approximate (the issue is Spring 2022).

works.author: stuart-russell
works.title: Make AI safe or make safe AI?
works.note: Solo, about 1,100 to 1,300 words (page updated 2025-09-23). Positions: post-hoc 'make AI safe' fixes do not work because developers do not understand their systems; 'make safe AI' with safety designed in and formal guarantees; regulators should put the burden of proof on developers; behavioural red lines (no self-replication, no breaking into systems, no bioweapon advice, no defamation); LLMs cannot demonstrably comply, and jailbreaks undermine red-teaming.

works.author: stuart-russell
works.title: DeepSeek, OpenAI, and the Race to Human Extinction
works.note: Solo, short (about 550 words); WebFetch noted an ellipsis gap mid-text, so it may be slightly truncated in the fetched view. Positions: DeepSeek's low cost challenges massive US compute spending; the data-centre buildup resembles a wasteful Cold War bomb race; the race to AGI is 'a race towards the edge of a cliff' because 'we have no idea how to control systems more intelligent than ourselves'. Covers the US-China rivalry.
